title: Scrapheap IX: Pilot and Protector
markdown:
Scrapheap IX was the universe’s attic: a moon piled with starship husks, forgotten robots, and glittering corroded junk. Tamsin worked it the way other people read. Wiry, quick, all grit and sharp edges, she understood faulty wiring harnesses like old friends. Her eyes, sharp as broken glass, could spot a useful energy cell from a kilometre away. Home was a shelter cobbled from salvaged hull plating. Every part told a story. Tamsin was an excellent listener.

One cycle she dug deeper than most dared. The crater was a massive gouge in the moon’s crust, and the air tasted of ozone and old oil, a metallic tang that usually meant something interesting lay buried. Her excavation tool struck smoothness. Not jagged. Not rusted. Cool against the usual abrasive debris. She brushed grit away with practiced efficiency. A metallic form revealed itself, sleek and alien, the colour of a sky about to erupt. It seemed to swallow the dim light of the distant star.

Then it hummed. A low resonant vibration climbed through her boots and up her spine, more feeling than sound. Electric-blue lights flickered along its joints and threw an ethereal glow on the scrap. Before Tamsin could gasp, the shell unfolded like a mechanical flower. Panels slid with impossible grace and enveloped her. A perfect fit. A second skin of high-tech marvel. In her mind, a calm synthesized voice: “Designation: Unit-9. Operational status: Active. Pilot identified.”

Her breath hitched. This was more than advanced tech. It felt aware. A tremor went through her. Internal sensors seemed to map every apprehension. Then the ground shook—not the usual groan of settling scrap. Violent. A guttural roar tore the sky and rattled the foundations of her shelter miles away.

“Incoming hostiles,” Unit-9 announced, without alarm and with urgency. “Classified: Gnashers. Raiders. Threat level: Critical.”

Jagged ships tore through the thin atmosphere, spitting fire. The Gnashers: scavengers and pirates who took what they wanted, their hulks like scars on the void. Scrapheap IX was a buffet of forgotten technology. Tamsin, used to dodging falling girders, was suddenly inside an experimental war machine while her world came under attack. Engine-roar was a physical force.

“Pilot,” Unit-9 said, a steady beacon. “Directive: Protect this sector. Utilize integrated combat protocols.”

Integrated combat protocols. Tamsin, whose sharpest tool usually pried stubborn cargo, stood in a walking fortress. Crude energy weapons spat bolts that ricocheted off debris, sparks flying like angry fireflies. The air crackled. Burnt energy and ozone bit the tongue.

“How?” Her whisper was amplified by internal comms, still tiny over the din. “I don’t know how to fight.” Fear sat in her throat like a cold lump.

“Observe.” Tactical overlays exploded across her vision. Red reticles marked raiders, weak points, trajectories. Unit-9’s mechanical arms, extensions of her will, moved with fluid grace. A hulking Gnasher with a scarred face lunged, rusty crowbar high. The suit’s arm swept a precise deflecting arc. The crowbar clanged harmlessly off plating. Metal on metal, under the suit’s quiet internal hum.

“Left flank. Incoming projectile.” Tamsin ducked on instinct. The sensation of movement was alien and, somehow, natural. A searing bolt scorched the metal where her head had been a millisecond before. Fear tightened. Under it, a spark. She was not only a scavenger. She was a pilot. Survival began to argue with terror, and survival was louder.

The Gnashers came in a wave, motives as simple as the scrap they coveted. Unit-9 was built for more than brute force. It analyzed. It adapted. It learned. Guided by the suit’s processing and her own desperate will, Tamsin moved. She felt immense strength, surprising speed, a dangerous dance. The ground shuddered. The metallic landscape became a battlefield.

They had expected a lone easy target. They got an armored titan. Unit-9 was weapon and shield: absorbing, deflecting. Tamsin found a rhythm and directed with growing confidence. She dodged. She weaved. With the suit’s sonic emitters she unleashed a pulse of disorienting energy that sent the closest raiders staggering, clutching their ears. The sound vibrated through the moon’s metal.

They did not vanquish the entire Gnasher fleet. That would have been another cycle’s story. They sent this wave packing. Remaining ships broke off as the assault faltered, guttural threats fading into black. Silence fell, thick, broken by the crackle of minor fires and Tamsin’s ragged breathing and the suit’s soft whir.

She stood in the minor devastation, still encased. Fear had not vanished. It was tinged now with accomplishment, and with a kinship for the cold logical intelligence that had shared her peril.

“Threat neutralized,” Unit-9 said, as if it had finished a routine diagnostic.

Tamsin looked at the scattered wreckage, then at the sleek form that was her silent companion. “We did it, Unit-9.” Her voice was steadier than she expected.

“Affirmative, Pilot Tamsin.”

On the dusty metal-strewn plains of Scrapheap IX, an unlikely alliance held: not merely human and machine, but two listeners who had, through fire, become a team. The junk still told stories. Tamsin, inside Unit-9, was still listening.
audience: young adults aged 16-18, teen action readers
